chunks.text: All right. Good morning, Mr. Short. You're here on behalf of Democracy Action Incorporated, is that correct? Yes, I am. Yes. Excellent. Good morning to you all Welcome along to the committee this morning. We've received your submission. We have 10 minutes set down for you. I'll hand over to you for introductory comments, and then I'm sure there'll be questions from members. Thank you. Thank you. Can you hear me okay?

Yes. Well, thank you, Mr. Chair and members of the committee, for the opportunity to appear today on behalf of Democracy Action. As you would have gathered from our written submission, while we support trade with India, our principal concern is the provision in the New Zealand Free Trade Agreement with India affirming the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, or UNDRIP.

We have received correspondence from the Minister of Trade, the Honorable Todd McClay, stating that the reference to UNDRIP in the agreement is not legally binding and does not impose any legal obligations on New Zealand. And while we welcome that assurance, we do not believe that is sufficient. Our concern is that the agreement formally affirms UNDRIP in legal and constitutional terms affirmation is significant.

It signals an acceptance of a commitment and can influence how courts and decision-makers interpret legislation and develop public policy. An express affirmation by New Zealand in an international agreement gives UNDRIP additional standing that it would not otherwise have. For that reason, we believe ministerial assurances alone are not adequate.

For instance, ministers change, governments change, and legislation endures. We believe nothing less than a clear statutory prohibition will provide the certainty that the Parliament intends. And fortunately, the solution already presents itself in the national interest analysis that accompanied the agreement.

Section 6 explains the new legislation and amendments to existing legislation are required to implement the bill and the agreement, and these measures will be contained in a single ominous bill. We therefore respectfully urge this committee to recommend that the implementing legislation include an explicit provision stating that the agreement affirmation of UNDRIP does not give UNDRIP the force of law in New Zealand, it does not create any rights or obligations under New Zealand law, and it does not give UNDRIP the presumptive weight in interpreting

legislation, and it does not make UNDRIP a relevant consideration for courts, ministers, public agencies or other decision-makers. For the avoidance of doubt, we further recommend the legislation state that for all purposes of New Zealand law, policy, and administrative practice, the agreement's affirmation of UNDRIP is to be disregarded.

Such a provision would remove uncertainty, give effect to the government's stated intention that the reference has no domestic legal effect, and prevent unnecessary litigation over Parliament's intent. We noted in our original submission that Rosemary Banks at the United Nations, when UNDRIP was put forward under the, uh, instructions of Helen Clark at the time, said that they would not sign it for the very reasons that have been outlined in our submission.

So we'd ask the committee to make these recommendations to the government. Thank you very much for your time. Excellent. All right. Do we have questions for Mr. Short in relation to his recommendations? I mean, very briefly, just at your oral submission here, you said that legislation endures. In fact, legislation can be passed very quickly in this Parliament, so I'm not quite sure that your statement that parliamentarians come and go and legislation endures is correct.

Is that a question? Well, governments change and then governments make decisions, don't they? And they can change things. So it would be good to have that in place. Thank you. Okay. So in relation to those clauses, sorry, did you have a proposal on where they should be im- implemented or inserted specifically?

Uh, yes, we had. That's in our submission under Section 6. Under Section 6 of? Sorry. Under Section 6 of the, um... Let's get the wording for you. It's in the national interest analysis which accompanies the agreement, Section 6 of that. Yes. Yeah, sorry, I mean in the legislation.

Did you have a view on where that should go? No. I, um, I'll leave that up to the people who draft the legislation, but it's appropriate that it goes in there. Okay. We're not actually asking for the, uh, Free Trade Agreement to be re- renegotiated. What we're saying is that in the supporting documentation that it should be included in that so it makes clear reference that UNDRIP has, has no effect on the New Zealand legislation.

Okay. So just adding those specific five recommendations as clauses within the enabling legislation to avoid any uncertainty. That's correct. Thank you. Okay. Very good. Any further questions for Mr. Short? All right. Thank you very much for your time this morning. Appreciate that.

Thank you. I appreciate the opportunity to, to present. Thank you. Okay. Next up, Export New Zealand and Business New Zealand Good morning. Good morning, Chair. Good morning, everybody. Morning. All right, welcome along. You know well how it works, so I'll hand straight over to you for your 10 minutes.

Sure. We've received your written submission. Thank you. I've just got a very short two-minute introduction- Sure... and then looking forward to questions. Thank you, Mr. Chair and members of the committee. My name's Katherine Rich, Chief Executive of Business New Zealand, and joining me today is Josh Tan, Executive Director of Export New Zealand. Thank you for the opportunity to appear in support of Business New Zealand and Export New Zealand's submission on the India Free Trade Agreement Legislation Amendment Bill.

Business New Zealand and Export New Zealand strongly support this bill because it contains the legislative changes needed for New Zealand to implement the India Free Trade Agreement. We encourage the committee to recommend that the bill proceed so that the agreement can enter into force as soon as practicable.

Business New Zealand and Export New Zealand have consistently supported closer economic ties with India for many, many years. We've previously presented our views on the agreement itself. Today, our focus is the legislation before the committee and the importance of implementing it without unnecessary delay.

From a business perspective, certainty and timing matter. This bill provides the legislative framework needed to give effect to the agreement and allow New Zealand businesses to begin accessing the commercial benefits. A powerful example of why this agreement matters is for the New Zealand's fish and seafood industry.

After Australia secured preferential access to India, its fish and seafood exports grew 269%, while New Zealand's exports fell by 67% over the same period. Under the NZFTA, the current 33% tariff on fish and seafood exports will be phased out over the next seven years.

Sheep meat and wool exporters, along with many others, will benefit from immediate duty-free access, significantly improving our competitiveness relative to Australia. We recognize that no trade agreement is perfect. There are areas where we would like to have seen more ambitious outcomes, particularly for dairy.

Nevertheless, the legislation enables an agreement that is commercially meaningful, strengthens New Zealand's relationship with one of the most important growing economies, and provides a foundation for future improvements. Our submission makes three recommendations. First, that the committee support the bill.

Secondly, that it progress through Parliament without delay. And thirdly, that the implementation is supported so exporters can fully utilize the opportunity the agreement creates. Thank you, and Josh and I welcome your questions. Wonderful. Thank you very much. Questions from members. Honorable David Benson.

Thank you very much for the submission, very clear. Yeah. The agreement includes a commitment to investment. Your members will probably be at the forefront of that. What advice are you giving to them, and how many have indicated that they are going to invest in India? Yes, you ask a very good question because free trade agreements are the start, and from there, it's how we utilize and make sure that businesses take advantage of that. So the message from Business New Zealand and Export New Zealand is that we in the business community work extremely

hard to make sure that we get on planes, send more delegations over, look at the market so we can access that 700 million odd growing middle class that wants our products and services. Just to supplement to that. How many have indicated that they are going to invest in India?

We don't have an actual number, but the feedback has been very positive. Most businesses that are export-focused looking at India understand the complexity of the market and the difficulty, but they see it as a long-term play, and many have started to put it into their export strategy. So Josh, do you wish to add?

Just feedback from our last barometer survey was that there was a sharp increase in the number of businesses that were interested in looking at India. I think from the discussions that we've had in and around the country, the market, because there has been quite high barriers in India, hasn't been an opportunity which exporters have looked at for the past several decades. Now that the free trade agreement is coming into play, there is an opportunity for them to start looking there.

So it is a long-term game for us. If I might add to that. Because we were put at such a competitive disadvantage in relation to Australia, there have been some that have shifted product from that market because they just simply could not compete. I think there is now an opportunity for some of those businesses to look back to India now that there's more of a level playing field.

Vanushi Walters. Thank you, and thank you both for your submissions. So I know you represent 76,000 employers and businesses, and your previous submission to consideration of the treaty, it's appended, you spoke about not holding any concerns regarding the labor mobility provisions. And I wonder if you could speak a little bit more to that and whether there are specific industries that are particularly appreciative of those settings in the trade deal.

Yes. We looked at- Very carefully at some of the comments being made publicly, and really did a deep dive into that area with regard to immigration and access to skills. And Josh has got some comments to make from that from our immigration specialist. So unfortunately, our policy manager couldn't be here with us today, but she said that mobility provisions are a normal part of trade agreements.

The business case is about enabling services, trade, skilled movement, business establishment, and commercial relationships, and that New Zealand does retain immigration policy control here. So we're quite confident that the mobility provisions are within the means of normal trade negotiations. Very good. Yes, Dr. Wilson.

My question is not about immigration. Under the investment, there has been some concern from a number of people I've spoken to that we're quite prepared to share our intellectual property with the likes of kiwifruit, our own cultivars that we've developed over years. We now notice also that India has got a very strong dairy sector, partially perhaps because we've shared intelligence and technology with them in the past. So there's a fear that with this new commitment to investment, a lot of our IP is subject to that as well.

Have you found that? Look, we respect the testing of ideas through the parliament and the different perspectives that are brought to bear in this discussion. But we don't share those fears, and particularly with regard to the dairy industry in India, we don't see that as a competition to New Zealand dairy farmers. Although, I think when you look at the sophistication of our industry here, yes, we do have some things to share around the globe. As we expressed, there was disappointment, of course, that this FTA does not

have significant dairy provisions in it. But we see this FTA as the beginning of a relationship that can develop over time, and we'd like to dream the big dream that over a period of time, that we can have those opportunities in there. Yeah, supplementary to just now flipping to horticulture and the idea that we're sharing our IP that's been grown in development through the likes of Food and Plant New Zealand, et cetera.

Is that something that you might be worried about because number are- We're not sharing IP for-- Are you suggesting we're sharing IP for free, or we're undertaking- It's part of the investment... commercial It's part of the investment commitment... activities there. Yeah. We looked also very carefully at the investment commitment, and it is an ambition to promote ongoing investment in India. And that actually makes sense because we sign these agreements not so much to have events and cut ribbons. Governments sign these agreements,

but it's the exporters that walk through the door and decide what within a country they can do to expand trade. So it's an ambitious target, but I think businesses are increasingly talking about the opportunities, and at least we're on a level playing field with our main competitors. Had we not done that, we would never catch up in that market.

Do you have confidence that the proposals outlined around the protection of IP, I think it's Annex 14A from memory, in terms of ensuring that no IP transfer happens until there is an appropriate system in country. Do you have confidence that that will give certainty or appropriate protections to any New Zealand exporters?

Look, I imagine when businesses are looking to do business, protection of IP and making sure that you can protect what is special about your business is something that all businesses do consider. You don't go and do business with someone if you feel you can't protect your trade secrets or your IP. So these will be the sorts of things that business weighs up when looking at trading with those markets.

But most businesses consider India as a very long-term play. Business relationships are absolutely key, and you only develop those over time. But IP is something that you would be discussing as part of any contractual arrangements. And certainly, those who are there consider these issues daily. Josh, anything to add to that?

What's up from Financial Alters? I was just wanting to confirm, just because Dr. Wilson suggested that there was a commitment to share IP as part of the investment clause of the agreement. I don't believe that that's the case, and so I just wanted to confirm. It was an area of, that's why I was asking- Yes... in terms of free sharing, that's not something that we- That's right... read into it.

Yes. The business will, as always, look at export markets, make judgments about the ability to serve those markets, and then go through every aspect of the business plan to make sure everything from IP protection through to labor through to margins, ability, supply- Mm-hmm... you name it, are part of that plan.

Sure. But overall, we see it as a terrific opportunity, and at least we can play catch up with Australia. Very good. Well, thank you both for your time this morning. Really appreciate your insights on behalf of Business New Zealand and Export NZ. Thanks. Okay, we come now to Zespri. Morning.

Morning. Chair and members of the committee, good morning, and thanks for the opportunity to appear today. My name is Rachel Lynch, and I'm the Government and Community Affairs Manager at Zespri. Zespri strongly supports the India Free Trade Agreement Legislation Amendment Bill and efforts to pass it before the election so that New Zealand kiwifruit growers can access the benefits of the free trade agreement from the next selling season next year.

India is one of the world's largest and fastest growing consumer markets. Zespri has operated in India for more than a decade, and demand for kiwifruit has continued to grow, driven by increasing consumer awareness of health and wellbeing and rising disposable incomes. During the last sales season, New Zealand exported around 7,500 tonnes to India, generating $32.7 million in sales revenue. Despite that growth, our exports have been constrained by the 33% tariff, and the FTA changes that. The tariff will be eliminated within a quota

of 6,250 tonnes from day one, growing to 15,000 tonnes over six years. Volumes outside the quota also benefit from a reduced tariff of 16.5%. For our growers, that's a huge improvement in access to an important trade market and allows us to allocate more fruit to India and build that demand over time.

And crucially, the quota is a foundation, not a ceiling. So Zespri will continue to allocate fruit based on demand, and long-term market opportunity, including above-quota allocations where that supports our market development. With clear execution, strong partnerships, and investment in the market, we hope and aim to see further improvements in access over time.

And that matters because we're in an incredibly challenging trading environment. Improved access and greater certainty are more important for exporters than ever, and the opportunity is substantial. With 1.4 billion people, even a fraction of those would be a whole lot of new consumers. And over time, India has the potential to become one of our largest markets, but that will take time and depend on careful execution.

Our written submission, as you would have seen, focuses on part four of the bill, which sets out the framework for the kiwifruit tariff quota system. We support the framework in part four and the appointment of our regulator, Kiwifruit New Zealand, as the quota manager. And we also appreciate the way that MPI has worked constructively with industry to design the allocation methodology and system.

The key points of that submission are pretty straightforward. Firstly, we support MPI's decision to reduce the new entrant allocation from 5 to 2.5%. We see that as a commercially viable volume for a new entrant while allowing, to maximize the value return to New Zealand growers. Secondly, we support the fair allocation and hand-back dates, including the 15 July hand-back date for those exporters who aren't able to use the full quota allocation.

Those predictable dates are really important given the commercial realities of the season, and make sure that New Zealand Inc. uses the quota that we have to the full benefit for all New Zealanders. Third, we support the quota volumes being reported in tonnes and ask that the regulations include a clear and consistent conversion to tray equivalents, which is our industry standard.

Fourth, we seek two modest amendments to the legislation itself. We ask that the quota manager's allocation processes are explicitly required to be cost-efficient, and the review process for allocation decisions should be affordable and timely given the commercial realities of the season. And finally, I want to briefly address the Kiwifruit Action Plan.

This is a cooperation program funded by New Zealand growers and delivered by our partners from BSI, our Bioeconomy Science Institute, and developed with a collective industry approach to support India's emerging green kiwifruit sector, which is counterseasonal to our own, meaning that the fruit is in market at broadly different times.

The program relates only to green kiwifruit. It does not include New Zealand providing any plant variety right material, and there is no transfer of protected commercial know-how. Protecting IP and plant variety rights was built into the program from the start, and it's a key part of why our industry is so supportive of it. The program is already underway with the development of two centers of excellence in Nagaland and Uttarakhand, training being delivered to growers and extension staff, and technical streams being planned and rolled out

for nursery, orchard, and post-harvest systems. Just to note too, the operating environment in these regions is challenging. The terrain is difficult, very mountainous, there are roading constraints and very limited post-harvest infrastructure. In our view, the Kiwifruit Action Plan shows how improved market access and practical industry cooperation can work together.

It supports local green kiwifruit growers in India, helps us get more Indian consumers buying more kiwifruit year-round, and protects New Zealand's IP and PPS. In closing, Zespri strongly supports the bill. We support the overall framework in part four and ask the committee to recommend a small number of targeted amendments reflected in our written submission.

We acknowledge and thank the officials involved in the negotiations and implementation work and ask that the focus is now on passing the legislation so that growers can benefit, uh, in the 2027 selling season. Thank you, and I welcome the questions. Excellent. Thank you, Rachel. Questions for Zespri? Dr David Dalton.

Yeah. Thank you very much for your submission, and also congratulations on the success of the industry. It's just unbelievably good. Thank you. Looking forward to this. Obviously, my question's going to be about the Kiwifruit Action Plan that you're- Oh, sure... investing. And, we're looking to provide training For growers, nursery. And obviously, cultivars will be part of that because they're the green kiwifruit, correct?

There's currently a green kiwifruit industry in- Yeah... India right now. The only plant material that is included in the program presently is rootstock- Right... which is not PBR. And we've got just over 100 plants that BSI is getting ready to send over.

And thank you also for your assurance that we're protecting gold and red. I know that's very important. Yeah. It's the why our industry, again, is so supportive of this too. Yeah. Okay, thank you. Very good. Rachel, I'm just interested if you could perhaps expand a little on your views around the need to be cost efficient- Mm... or to be proportionate- Yeah... with the cost recovery piece and how you would define that for us.

Sure. Kiwifruit New Zealand is already our regulator and has an obligation to provide services to the industry that are cost efficient. So we would just like that reflected, again, in the legislation here. And in terms of being timely, we need quick decisions in our industry.

The commercial realities are that volumes can change week by week. So we would want to have, in the legislation, an acknowledgement that any decisions as things change would need to be both timely and cost effective-... just so we can allocate and reallocate them as quickly as we need to.

Okay. So just on that timeliness, a note under the Clause 51, which is the process around reviewing a decision to cancel or suspend an export license. Mm. There's a timeframe in there for anyone wanting to have a review of decision made against them. Mm.

Then there's a review of that, which is not a prescribed timeframe, and then there is an appeal mechanism which is prescribed again. Mm. So I'm interested in whether you feel that there should be a timeframe for the review process as well, because obviously that would enable a potential reallocation of- Mm... supplies if that review was not successful.

Perhaps that's something that would be better in the regulations as we figure out the realities of how that would work in practice, rather than have it in the leg, which is harder to change if we discover that things don't quite work as we thought they were going to. Mm. Okay. So across all of those as that review piece in terms of the original complaint, the review, and the potential- Yeah... appeal, that would be better prescribed in regulations- I think so... all three of those?

Yeah. Okay. Thank you. Vanisha Walters. Thank you, Mr. Chair. And mine is actually a supplementary- Mm... in relation to the cost-efficient provision. Mm. Appreciate that there's clarity in having it in primary legislation. We also have regulatory impact assessments- Yes... which require that cost/benefit analysis as well.

And so that will apply to all secondary legislation. Mm. And I'm just wondering whether that is, in terms of legislative harmony-... an easier way of ensuring all our secondary leg- Mm... has that cost/benefit assessment which currently happens, and that way we're not putting it in primary legislation across the board.

Yeah. That could potentially- Cover it... we're just wanting to- Make sure it's there... confirm that it's covered. Yeah. It's a good point to raise. Thank you. All right, any further questions? No, that's good. Wonderful. Thank you very much- Thanks so much... Rachel, on behalf of Kiwifruit. Okay, next up, we have Sovereign.

Good morning. Yeah, hi, Tim. Joining us-... on behalf of Sovereign. Thanks, Tim. Wonderful. Thanks. Yeah, my submission will address Clauses 47 and 66 and the treaty obligations that they activate. This bill enables ratification, and ratification activates every provision that I will reference.

First, just a foreword on what I think are the committee's shortcomings from the first round of oral submissions and their report to Parliament. The committee's treaty examination report failed to examine the Motu report's trade diversion finding. It addressed Annex 8K, but dismissed submitter concerns, stating that it will not change immigration flows in the ways that submitters think they will, without acknowledging Article VIII (3) (4) , which says that those ICT visas are uncap able.

That provision also prohibits caps on labor market tests and salary floors, which the UK has, but they were also inundated with Indian visas under a very similar ICT visa scheme. We don't have the ability to cap those. MPs then relied on that incomplete report to justify their votes, while their own representations in Parliament omitted the same critical details.

This bill hearing is the last opportunity to put on record what the treaty examination report missed. Every step of this process has been designed- Mr. Riley, this process-... now is actually about the legislation in front of us to give effect to the- Sure, sure. I understand that. Yeah, yeah... the comments need to focus around the legislation and stuff rather than the treaty process.

Yeah. This was import-- Yeah, I just thought this was important context because Sovereign doesn't feel that the committee did a thorough job at reporting to Parliament what the treaty actually does to New Zealand. So yeah, I'll just start with Clause 47, which is the quota on horticulture, on kiwifruit, apples, and honey.

This clause creates quotas on horticulture exports to India, which are conditional and suspendable Clause 47, as I said, creates the quota systems for apples, kiwi fruit, and honey. Annex 2B.9 of the FTA says that India alone can suspend the access. So we're setting up legislation that didn't exist before.

This is new legislation, and it is conditional on an action plan that is not yet in place. The legislation and the FTA relies on several things being set up, which includes cultivar transfer to India. We have to set up centers of excellence and set up PVR framework. And we just heard Zespri speaking to their confidence in the IP protection that India will give us, but none of that was stipulated in the FTA.

It just says that New Zealand needs to work with India to set up their IP. And that's because India, they're not a UPOV member. Zespri only trades with UPOV countries. They haven't traded with India because they are not a UPOV member. That's International Protection of Premium Varieties. We expect that India will do something in regards to IP to amend this, but nothing in the FTA required that.

So we have about a quarter or more of our trade, which is horticulture, and it is totally contingent on India setting up an IP framework that's compatible with New Zealand. It's also contingent on the transfer of our cultivars. Zespri also mentioned BSI's work. BSI said that India will be able to produce 10 times their current kiwi production given our skills and the cultivars that will be transferred in the FTA.

So we're creating a massive competitor, a country that is known on the USTR list to be a priority watchlist member, alongside Russia, China, and Venezuela for IP violations. So we're setting up legislation, and we're going to activate these provisions of the FTA, which do not protect at the moment New Zealand's IP and our horticulture.

That is the heart and soul of our horticulture industry. It's the development of our germplasm, our cultivars, and our premium varieties over decades, and at a cost of about $100 million thus far. Then we'll go to Clause 66, which is the Immigration Act commitments. This clause enables Annex 8K, which I mentioned before, I referenced.

This is the uncappable pathway. This is the intra-corporate transfer visas. Specifically, the specialists have no cap. The treaty says that we cannot place caps on these visas. The committee looked at that and said, "We're not too concerned about it." But they failed to understand that ICTs in this treaty are very similar to ICTs in the UK.

Those ICTs were exploited prolifically, and the UK had to clamp down. They did so by increasing the salary minimum for these visas. New Zealand doesn't have that ability, and the FTA specifically prevents us from putting salary caps. So when the committee says that we're not concerned because similar provisions are in other FTAs, they don't understand that we are dealing with India, a country known for exploitation of visas in the UK and in the United States.

That means we've got a country of 1.4 billion people that we open the door to specialist transfers. We have no ability to put the same levers in place that the UK used to stop the exploitation of the very similar type of visa in the UK. I believe that the committee needs to look at this closer, and by enabling Clause 66, they enabled this door through the 8K visa into New Zealand.

And then I'll just go to the FDI commitment that Zespri also mentioned just before me. Or it was the submitter just before her, actually. The FDI commitment is $20 billion into New Zealand in 15 years. And last time I addressed this committee, I asked if anybody knew the total outward FDI commitment to all countries worldwide combined up to this date, and that number is 16 billion. And I said it's impossible for New Zealand to achieve the $20 billion FDI commitment.

And the committee went to MFAT, and MFAT agreed, yes. It said specifically that New Zealand cannot invest $20 billion into India, but that that's only a promotion. So if we're agreeing to promote $20 billion into India, a number that MFAT says is not possible, which I backed up in my last oral presentation, what are we doing? How can we prove to India that we have promoted an unachievable amount of investment into India?

That is so abstract. And so now everything that this FTA gives us, which is the tariff concessions, that's all we get. We give India our cultivars, we give it our $20 billion. The only thing we get back are tariffs. Those tariffs are contingent on this FDI commitment, which is largely undefined. India alone decides whether or not we met that commitment. They take our tariffs, the entire FTA falls apart.

All of our investment up to that point is garbage. It's wasted. And then there's a five-year review. So after five years, India can come back and say, "Oh, did you meet the FDI commitment?" If we don't, there's another review after three years and three years for eternity. So what company is going to continue investing into India if our tariffs are clawed back at the first 15-year check?

We will never reach that goal. And this hands India sole discretion over this FTA, sole discretion to take back our tariffs. I think that's an oversight. If somebody came to you and had a similar deal for you to purchase something, you would say absolutely no, this is ridiculous. But for some reason, this committee pretends like this is normal and this is fine.

And I think the committee needs to understand that they serve the country first and not their party leader and not their party. It is the country first, and this is not in New Zealand's best interest. This is negotiated directly against New Zealand. We have no cards in this game. Any questions? All right. Well, thank you very much for hearing your perspective on that.

Are there any questions for Mr. Riley? No. Mr. Riley, you may wish to look at Article 14A32C and 5B, which speak clearly to the protections around IP that may be useful to address some of your concerns. Well, but yeah. Thank you very much for your time online. Can I just write a reply to that? The protect- No, you've already said that they're not protected.

Those clauses clearly state they are, so- I want to explain why those clauses don't protect- We appreciate your time. Why would you... I still have a couple minutes. I think I'd like to finish off. And we will move on to our next submitter. He barely has time. Can he respond to what you've just said? No. No, we're at time. We're at time.
Our next submitter, Rex Landing.

Thanks, Rachel. Do we hear from Stanley? It's Max Marshall, but I've bumped you. I'm not sure who's on next. Potentially, what have we? We might have to wait for Watson. Okay. Watson Reynolds. So we had Rex Landing, next then Metals New Zealand.

No? Just the updated one is- Oh, it's updated as- Is Craig Atkinson? Yes. Craig was- Craig's not on yet. Craig was on the side. So Max Marshall. Max Marshall is next, and then it would be Metals New Zealand, who we also don't have. But we do have Cody Quince in the Zoom. All right. Well, let's proceed there.
Okay, Cody Quince online.
Yeah, okay.

Good morning. You can hear us all right, can you? Morning. Yes, we can hear you. Can you hear us? Yes, thank you. Wonderful. Yeah. Okay. Thank you for bringing your time forward a little bit. We have received your written submission and supplementary contributions to that, and we'll hand over to you for five minutes.

Thank you. I'm adding to my written submission today because I believe critical new evidence has come to light. I think official advice evaluated these trade clauses in isolation but missed how they interact in the real world. To fix that, I put together an independent risk audit using financial modeling, a high court insolvency records, and public trade data. I have formally provided your secretary with a 100-page strategic risk dossier containing 24 detailed risks alongside with a suggested

statutory clause. I cannot go over all 24 risks in five minutes, so I'm focusing on one of the biggest structural risks I've found and the exact fix the committee can adopt to solve it. I urge you to read the dossier in your own time and adopt the total control certificate as suggested in the clause provided.

First, public data shows our growers are carrying record debt. Bank debt with Zespri SunGold license prices previously peaked over 800,000 a hectare. Crown officials call Chapter 9's 33 billion investment target aspirational, but India's commerce minister treats it as a strict baseline.

That is why Chapter 9 includes a mandatory five-year review clause. It isn't a polite check-in, it's an enforcement milestone. If New Zealand fails to send 2.2 billion in outward capital to India every single year, that five-year review gives India the leverage to pull back tariff concessions.

When private capital falls short, the pressure snaps straight back onto the debt-burdened growers. Second, financial pressure drives foreign syndicates to bypass buying sensitive land outright. Instead, they build unscreened control over our critical export infrastructure through commercial leases on industrial land, taking over pack houses, cool stores, and port storage in separate sub $200 million deals, like Seeker

$60 million acquisition of OPAC because industrial land is not classified as a sensitive land. The Overseas Investment Office screens zero of these commercial leases. This lets foreign entities aggregate control over strategic supply chains without checks Local Kiwis have to follow.
